newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles battle flood damage, dry weather forecast.
newsitem.headline: Poles battle flood damage, dry weather forecast.

text.p: Poles, exhausted by two weeks of floods that devastated much of the country's south, took comfort from weather forecasts on Monday that the worst deluge in centuries was nearing an end.

Some communities still battled encroaching water. Others laboured in the debris and mud to repair damage which analysts say may cost Poland several billion dollars and affect forthcoming parliamentary elections.

"Despite rains on Sunday and on Monday, the situation is much better than it was and everything suggests it will improve," Krzysxtof Pomes, Poland's flood crisis committee spokesman, told Reuters. "Water levels are tending to subside on most rivers."

Rain lashing the flood-stricken region of Silesia on Monday would gradually subside until Wednesday and the rest of the week was likely to be sunny, said Anna Nemec of the state Meteorology and Water Management Institute.
Some areas in southwest and south Poland remained under the floodwater that has inundated more than 1,000 towns and villages.
The death toll had reached at least 52 people, police said, while 140,000 had been forced to evacuate their homes.

A flood wave caused by the earlier downpour was storming along the Odra river on the German border towards the northwestern port of Szczecin but was unlikely to swamp the city, flood control officials said.
Poland's biggest river, the Wisla, was calm. Smaller mountain rivers overflowed in Nowy Sacz and Jelenia Gora provinces, where floods may still hit some towns and villages.

Residents of the damaged areas along with about 50,000 troops and fire fighters, were working hard to contain the damage. Food, water, clothes, and cleaning materials were flowing from all over the country and charity events were staged nationwide.
"People are working themselves into a sweat. Many of them lost all their possessions," Grzegorz Ossowski, a local radio reporter in the southwestern city of Walbrzych, told Reuters.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski increasingly thought a state of emergency in the worst-hit areas, which would postpone general elections due on September 21, was unnecessary, his spokesman said.
"The final decision has not been taken. But there are less and less circumstances that could compel the president to impose the measure," Antoni Styrczula said.
The right-wing opposition has demanded that the emergency be introduced to help freeze prices and speed up decision making.

The ruling ex-communists, who will be challenged by the Solidarity alliance (AWS) during the September 21 polls, found themselves on the defensive after media and politicians' accusations that they had mishandled the relief operation.
The government met to discuss final points of its plan to help flood victims and rebuild wrecked infrastructure. Officials said it would make binding decisions on Tuesday.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told reporters before the meeting the plan would be in three phases.

These were immediate disease prevention and relief for victims, a medium term plan for rebuilding roads, bridges and telecommunications, followed by a long-term flood control effort to build or improve reservoirs and dykes as well as provide better warning systems.

The government flood relief office chief, Andrzej Pilat, said earlier the government had gathered about $1 billion for the programme and had parliament's approval to borrow up to another $730 billion from the central bank for the purpose.
